summary: Defines Multicast VPN extensions letting downstream provider edges consider the status of provider tunnels when picking the upstream PE for a multicast flow. Using Bidirectional Forwarding Detection for multipoint tunnels, they can switch fast on upstream failures.

eli5.summary: If the main path to a live video source breaks, receivers quickly switch to a backup, since they keep checking.

questions: mvpn upstream pe selection with bfd
what is the bfd discriminator bgp attribute
what is the standby pe community
subtitle: Letting multicast VPN receivers notice a dead upstream tunnel and switch to a standby source router quickly.

tldr.problem: In a multicast VPN, a receiving provider edge router can keep waiting on a failed upstream router or tunnel until slow routing updates catch up.
tldr.mechanism: Downstream PEs consider the status of each provider tunnel when choosing the Upstream PE, optionally tracked with multipoint BFD and a new BFD Discriminator BGP attribute. A new Standby PE BGP community lets a C-multicast route be sent toward a standby Upstream PE ahead of time.
tldr.outcome: Operators can choose cold, warm or hot standby so that failover needs little or no multicast routing exchange at recovery time. The procedures are optional.

today: RFC 9026 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2021, and its metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. Its procedures are optional extensions to the multicast VPN specifications RFC 6513 and RFC 6514.

sections.title: Fast Recovery for Multicast VPNs
sections.content:
The RFC assumes the reader knows multicast in BGP/MPLS IP VPNs from RFC 6513 and RFC 6514. It targets failures of elements in the provider network that are upstream of the PEs connected to VPN sites with receivers.

It has three pieces. Section 3 lets an egress PE take the status of provider tunnels (P-tunnels) into account when it picks the Upstream Multicast Hop (UMH) for a (C-S,C-G). Section 4 defines an optional BGP extension, a new Standby PE community, so that failover needs no MVPN routing message exchange at recovery time. Section 5 combines both into a hot root standby mechanism, which the RFC says has similarities with the approach of RFC 7431 for PIM.

All of this is optional. A BGP implementation that does not recognize or is configured not to support the extensions keeps providing multicast service as in RFC 6513.
sections.eli5: Some people watch a live stream through a network of pipes. This document adds optional tricks so that when a pipe breaks, the viewers switch to a spare one fast. If a router does not know the tricks, things still work the old way.

sections.title: Choosing the Upstream PE by Tunnel Status
sections.content:
For a downstream PE and a VRF, the P-tunnel for a given Upstream PE is the S-PMSI tunnel that PE advertised for the (C-S,C-G), or the I-PMSI tunnel if there is no S-PMSI. The optional procedure leaves a PE out of the list of candidate UMHs when its tunnel is Down, so the downstream PE fails over to the next candidate. If a tunnel's status cannot be determined, it is treated as 'not known to be Down' and may be used.

The RFC applies this to the three UMH selection options of RFC 6513. For the first two (IP address or hashing), a candidate is kept if its tunnel is not known to be Down, or if it advertises no applicable x-PMSI but has a VRF Route Import extended community on its unicast VPN route for the source. If the set ends up empty, selection is repeated without looking at tunnel status. For the third (the installed UMH route), the best route among PEs whose tunnel is not down is chosen, falling back to the installed route if there is none.

Status is not a property of the tunnel itself but how it looks from one particular downstream PE, since a failure may hit only some branches.
sections.eli5: Each receiver keeps a list of possible senders and crosses off any whose pipe looks broken. If every name gets crossed off, it just goes back to using the full list.

sections.title: Ways to Decide a Tunnel Is Down
sections.content:
An implementation may support any combination of these methods and let the operator choose.

  • Tunnel root tracking: is the root in the x-PMSI Tunnel attribute reachable in unicast routing? Similar to BGP next-hop tracking.
  • PE-P upstream link status: is the last-hop link of the P-tunnel Up? With fast reroute in place, detection intervals need coordination; the RFC recommends longer intervals at higher layers and gives 10 msec for the link and at least 100 msec for the tunnel as an example.
  • P2MP RSVP-TE tunnels: Up if the sub-LSP to this PE is Up. When it goes Down, the ingress PE MUST NOT be a valid candidate UMH.
  • Leaf-initiated P-tunnels: an Upstream PE MUST be removed from the candidate list if a leaf-triggered (PIM, mLDP) tunnel branch cannot be built.
  • (C-S,C-G) counters: infer a failure when packets stop arriving within the maximum inter-packet time. A configurable timer MUST wait for any tunnel restoration, and three seconds is described as a generally suitable default.
  • BFD Discriminator: track a multipoint BFD session, described in the next section.

The operational notes say BFD may give the most accurate and expedient notification but adds load, so operators should weigh the rate of BFD Control packets and the number of sessions. Root tracking is based on the control plane, which does not fate-share with the MPLS data plane, so it can raise false alarms.
sections.eli5: There are many ways to tell if a pipe is broken: ask if the far end can still be reached, check the last link, or simply notice that the water stopped flowing. The best one sends a tiny 'still here' ping all the time.

sections.title: BFD Discriminator and Multipoint BFD
sections.content:
This RFC defines a new optional transitive BGP attribute, BFD Discriminator, code point 38. It has a 1-octet BFD Mode (value 1 means P2MP BFD Session), a 4-octet BFD Discriminator and optional TLVs. A Source IP Address TLV (type 1) MUST be present when the mode is P2MP; its length is 4 for IPv4 and 16 for IPv6 and it holds the address of the MultipointHead. The attribute is malformed if shorter than 11 octets or if TLVs are malformed, and then the UPDATE is handled by attribute discard per RFC 7606.

The Upstream PE starts a BFD session with bfd.SessionType = MultipointHead (RFC 8562), sends BFD Control packets over the P-tunnel with inner destination address 127.0.0.1/32 (or ::1/128 for IPv6), uses the TLV address as the source, and puts the discriminator in the x-PMSI A-D Route.

The downstream PE associates the discriminator with the tunnel and Upstream PE, creates a MultipointTail session, and demultiplexes using the TLV address, the discriminator and the x-PMSI Tunnel Identifier. When the session is Down or AdminDown, or its Detection Timer expires, the tunnel MUST be considered down. The downstream PE MAY then switch to the Standby Upstream PE only if that PE is deemed Up.

For PE-CE link failure, the Upstream PE MUST set bfd.LocalDiag to Concatenated Path Down or Reverse Concatenated Path Down so downstream PEs treat it as a tunnel failure, unless it moves to a new PE-CE link within bfd.DesiredMinTxInterval.
sections.eli5: The sender keeps shouting 'I am here' down the pipe, and a note in the announcement says which shout to listen for. If the shouting stops, the receivers know something broke, even if the pipe itself looks fine.

sections.title: Standby C-Multicast Routes
sections.content:
This applies when the site holding the source (C-S) connects to two or more PEs. A downstream PE picks a Primary Upstream PE; the other is the Standby Upstream PE. All PEs of the MVPN must use the same UMH selection. Revertive behavior (return to the Primary when it recovers) MUST be supported and is the default; non-revertive MAY also be supported, but the choice MUST be consistent on all PEs.

When both are reachable, the downstream PE sends its normal C-multicast route and also a Standby C-multicast route. Its NLRI matches the primary route except the RD is the one that would be used with the Standby PE as UMH, and it MUST carry the Standby PE community (0xFFFF0009). Its LOCAL_PREF must be lower than that of the normal route; zero is RECOMMENDED. The PE that advertises it MUST join the corresponding P-tunnel. If the Primary becomes unreachable, the PE resends the route toward the Standby PE without the community.

An Upstream PE that gets a Standby route, and finds the source unreachable through another PE, MAY install VRF PIM state and MAY forward traffic. Local policy decides how far to go. Doing neither is cold root standby, joining the CE side without forwarding is warm root standby, and forwarding to other PEs through the P-tunnel is hot root standby.

For inter-AS use, with two or more Inter-AS I-PMSI A-D Routes with distinct RDs, a downstream PE builds a second, Standby, route from a second route. ASBRs that support this MUST be configurable to translate between LOCAL_PREF zero over iBGP and MED 0xffff over eBGP.
sections.eli5: A receiver tells both the main sender and a spare sender it wants the show, but marks the request to the spare as 'only if needed'. The spare can wait quietly, warm up, or already send the show, depending on how fast you want the switch.

sections.title: Hot Root Standby and Duplicate Packets
sections.content:
Combining the two mechanisms gives hot root standby. Downstream PEs advertise Standby C-multicast routes, Upstream PEs use the hot standby behavior and forward after receiving a primary or standby route, and a policy controls which tunnel downstream PEs accept traffic from, for example based on the status of the tunnel. The RFC notes that a plain C-multicast Source Tree Join sent to both Upstream PEs would give the same protection, but the Standby semantic lets the operator change the protection level on the secondary Upstream PE alone, without reconfiguring all downstream PEs.

Because two Upstream PEs may then send the same traffic at once, the rule in RFC 6513 that a PE forwards to CEs only packets from the expected Upstream PE matters especially. The RFC says this can also happen when downstream PEs judge tunnel status differently.
sections.eli5: If both senders send the show at once, the receiver must only show one copy, the one from the sender it chose.

sections.title: IANA Allocations
sections.content: IANA allocated the BGP Standby PE community value 0xFFFF0009 (First Come First Served) and code point 38 in the BGP Path Attributes registry for BFD Discriminator. It created two subregistries in the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) Parameters registry: BFD Mode, where value 1 is P2MP BFD Session, and BFD Discriminator Optional TLV Type, where value 1 is Source IP Address. In both, 0 and 255 are Reserved, 0 to 175 and 255 follow IETF Review, 176 to 249 are First Come First Served and 250 to 254 are Experimental Use.
sections.eli5: The special labels used by this feature were written into the official public lists so they stay unique.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The procedures share the security considerations of RFC 6513 and RFC 6514, and of P2MP BFD in RFC 8562 and RFC 5880. An implementation MUST provide a way to limit the overall capacity used by BFD traffic, counting both active sessions and the rate of BFD Control packets to process. The tunnel-status methods may also give false-negative state changes that trigger needless control-plane convergence, so operators are expected to use the available controls.
sections.eli5: The 'I am here' pings must be capped so they cannot flood the routers, and a false alarm can cause a pointless switch.

fields.desc: The My Discriminator value of the BFD session.

viz.caption: WHAT THE STANDBY UPSTREAM PE DOES WITH A STANDBY ROUTE

items.label: Cold root standby
items.desc: Neither installs PIM state toward the source nor forwards traffic until needed.

items.label: Warm root standby
items.desc: Installs VRF PIM state and receives traffic, but does not forward it to other PEs.

items.label: Hot root standby
items.desc: Also forwards traffic to other PEs over its P-tunnel.
